When the air turns: forecasting PM2.5 through wildfire smoke

A benchmark of 14 forecasting methods on 538 US air quality monitors, fixed before the record 2023 smoke season and tested through it. The question is what holds up when the data stop looking like the training set.

Data: US EPA Air Quality System, hourly PM2.5, 2021 to 2024. 35.6 million raw readings, 17.8 million forecast-hours scored. Everything on this page is produced by python run.py all.

1. The question

In June 2023 smoke from Canadian wildfires gave New York, Philadelphia, Chicago and Detroit some of the worst air ever measured there. Little in the previous two years of data looked like it. That makes it a clean natural experiment for a question every deployed model eventually faces: what happens when the world leaves the training distribution?

Several families of forecaster are compared on identical forecasts: naive rules, gradient-boosted trees, a transformer trained from scratch, and pretrained foundation models used zero-shot. Each trained model comes with and without information from neighbouring monitors, which isolates the value of spatial context.

2. The data, and how far 2023 moved

The EPA files hold one row per instrument per hour: 35,615,837 rows in all, covering 954 sites in the contiguous US. Sites are kept if they reported at least 85% of hours in every one of the four years, which leaves 538 monitors and 18,287,581 hourly observations (3.1% of cells missing). Missing hours are never filled in the targets.

Region2021202220232024Tail (99.9th percentile) in 2023 vs trainingMonitors with more unhealthy hours in 2023 than 2022
Northeast0.57%0.27%1.57%0.14%2.77x98%
Midwest1.04%0.32%2.02%0.39%1.99x98%
South0.45%0.36%0.89%0.58%1.42x78%
West2.62%1.50%1.10%0.98%0.75x34%

The change is not a statistical subtlety. Comparing each monitor with itself, 98% of Northeast monitors had more unhealthy hours in 2023 than in 2022 (median 130 hours against 6; paired Wilcoxon test, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001).

The shift lives in the tail. A standard drift statistic on the whole distribution, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance from the training period, is 0.033 for the Northeast in 2023 and 0.102 in 2024. Read alone, it says the quiet year 2024 moved further than the smoke year. The 99.9th percentile says the opposite: 2.8 times the training value in 2023, 0.6 times in 2024. Monitoring the bulk of a distribution would have missed the event that mattered.

3. Smoke has spatial structure

CityDistance from Minneapolis, kmTrails Minneapolis by, hoursPeak PM2.5, µg/m³
Chicago541+2222
Detroit864+24197
Cleveland1029+26225
Pittsburgh1194+22221
Washington DC1498+26119
Philadelphia1582+49126
New York1648+50100

Lagged cross-correlation puts numbers on the picture: the series at each city lines up best with Minneapolis when shifted by the hours shown. A monitor's own history cannot contain a plume that has not arrived, but a monitor a few hundred kilometres upwind already does. That is the case for giving models spatial context.

A multiple-testing aside

Does PM2.5 differ between weekdays and weekends? Testing each of the 538 monitors separately gives 58 "significant" results at p < 0.05, where about 27 are expected by chance alone. Controlling the false discovery rate at 5% (Benjamini-Hochberg) leaves 4, and Bonferroni leaves 3. Unlike traffic gases, fine particles show almost no weekly cycle, and uncorrected testing would have invented one.

4. The benchmark protocol

  • Task. Every day at 12:00 UTC, each model forecasts the next 48 hours at every monitor, using at most the previous 168 hours. 729 issue days, 375,426 forecasts.
  • Split by time. Models learn from data before 2022-07-01. July to December 2022 is for early stopping and tuning. 2023 and 2024 are the test: one smoke year, one ordinary year. No training target overlaps the validation or test period.
  • Same cells for everyone. A forecast-hour counts only if every model produced a number for it and the truth was observed.
  • Three scores. MAE in µg/m³; MASE, which scales by each monitor's own difficulty; and weighted quantile loss (WQL) for the nine predicted quantiles.
  • Uncertainty in the comparison itself. Intervals on relative error come from resampling whole days, since a plume makes errors at different monitors on the same day strongly dependent.
  • Leakage tests. Twelve automated checks, including ones that corrupt all data after a cut-off and assert that no feature, model input or baseline before it changes.
ModelWhat it is
PersistenceThe latest reading, repeated for 48 hours
Seasonal naiveThe same clock hour on the latest observed day
Damped persistenceSeven-day hourly profile plus a decaying share of the current anomaly (one fitted number per horizon)
XGBoostGradient-boosted trees on the monitor's own history; one global model, nine quantiles
XGBoost + neighboursThe same, plus 16 features describing monitors up to 800 km away
XGBoost (level label)Ablation of the first tree model: predicts the level instead of the change from the latest reading
TransformerPatch transformer trained from scratch in PyTorch on the monitor's own history
Transformer + neighboursThe same, plus two neighbour input channels
Chronos-BoltAmazon's 2024 pretrained forecasting model, zero-shot, same 168-hour context
Chronos-2Amazon's 2025 pretrained forecasting model, zero-shot, same 168-hour context
Chronos-2 (long context)Chronos-2 given 21 days of history
TimesFMGoogle's pretrained forecasting model (version 2.5), zero-shot, same 168-hour context
EnsembleEqual-weight average of the two neighbour-aware trained models; nothing fitted
Ensemble + foundationEqual-weight average of those two plus Chronos-2 and TimesFM; nothing fitted

The tree models were tuned by random search on the validation period (10 settings; the best improved validation loss by 0.3% over the defaults, so tuning was not where the gains were). The tree model with neighbours trained on 2,164,300 rows on a GPU; the transformer has 1,641,392 parameters and trained for 10 epochs on a GPU.

  • Models trained on this data beat every naive rule, and the intervals do not touch 1.0. The best single model, XGBoost + neighbours, has 13% lower error than damped persistence.
  • Trees and the transformer are close overall (3.51 and 3.52 µg/m³ with neighbours). With smoke present at issue the ranking is clearer: Transformer + neighbours is best at 8.99 µg/m³.
  • Averaging the two families helps. The ensemble fits nothing and scores 3.46 overall, better than either member, which is what happens when two models make different errors.
  • The smoke year was harder for every method. Ensemble has an MAE of 3.83 µg/m³ in 2023 and 3.09 in 2024. The learned models stay ahead of every naive rule in both years.
  • Plain persistence is a poor forecast in smoke: 38% worse than damped persistence when smoke is present at issue. Smoke episodes end, and a forecast that assumes they will not pays for it.

6. The slicing trap

A natural way to ask "which model is best in smoke?" is to score only the hours that turned out to be elevated. On this dataset that puts plain persistence first and moves every zero-shot model ahead of every model trained on the data.

ModelMAE on hours that turned out elevatedRankMAE when smoke was present at issueRank

Scored on elevated outcomes, persistence ranks 1 of 14. Scored on a stratum that is known when the forecast is issued, it ranks 13. Both columns use the same forecasts. The first selects cases by what happened, which rewards any forecast that leans high: if only bad outcomes are scored, a forecaster that always predicts bad air looks skilled. This is known as the forecaster's dilemma (Lerch et al., 2017), and it is easy to fall into when a team reports "performance on the hard examples".

All rankings in this report use strata defined at issue time. Outcome-selected slices appear only to show where the damage is, never to choose a model.

7. Zero-shot foundation models

Pretrained forecasting models promise good forecasts with no training on the target data. They were given exactly the same input as the other own-history models, the last 168 hours of one monitor, and asked for the same nine quantiles. Nothing about them was fitted or tuned here.

One caution applies to this section only. These models were released in 2024 and 2025 and their pretraining data are not fully documented, so they may have seen time series from 2023 or 2024. The trained models in this benchmark provably saw nothing after June 2022; the foundation models carry no such guarantee.

The best of them on equal terms, TimesFM, reaches an MAE of 3.78 µg/m³ without having seen a single reading from this dataset. That is 4.5% higher than Transformer (3.62), the best model trained here on the same information, and 6% lower than damped persistence. With smoke present at issue its MAE is 10.04, against 9.35 for Transformer and 8.99 for Transformer + neighbours, the best of all methods in that stratum.

Giving a model three weeks of history instead of one: Chronos-2 goes from 3.92 to 3.78 µg/m³.

Adding Chronos-2 and TimesFM to the two trained neighbour-aware models, with equal weights chosen before any of them was scored, moves the ensemble's MAE from 3.462 to 3.539 µg/m³ overall and from 9.13 to 9.34 with smoke present at issue.

For onset warnings, with the shared 168-hour input the foundation models score a PR-AUC between 0.13 and 0.15, the same range as the trained models that see only one monitor (0.12 to 0.16). With three weeks of history, Chronos-2 reaches 0.19. The best neighbour-aware model, Transformer + neighbours, reaches 0.26. Pretraining on a very large collection of other series does not tell a model that smoke is 300 km away.

8. What neighbours add

For average accuracy the gain is steady but small: 3.2% lower MAE for the tree model and 2.8% for the transformer, and 3.9% and 3.9% with smoke present at issue. For warning that a clean day is about to turn unhealthy the gain is large: PR-AUC rises by a factor of 1.7 for the trees and 1.7 for the transformer. Spatial context matters most exactly where a monitor's own history is silent.

A design choice that mattered less than expected

The tree models predict the change from the latest reading. The reasoning was that trees cannot output a value beyond the range of their training labels, so a model trained on levels would be capped in an unprecedented episode. The ablation supports the reasoning only at the extremes. On hours above 125 µg/m³ the level model is too low by 170 µg/m³ on average, against 146 for the change model. But in the fair smoke stratum the level model is slightly better (9.65 against 10.06 µg/m³), and overall the two differ by 0.4%. A sound argument about extremes did not turn into a better forecast on average, which is the reason to run the ablation instead of trusting the argument.

9. One episode, up close

No model forecast the peak of 7 to 8 June. The morning before it, readings were moderate and every method predicted more of the same. Once the smoke was there, the methods differ in how they let go of it. On the morning of 8 June, with the worst already past, the tree model holds the level for a full day and the transformer decays towards normal, which is what happened. The two foundation models give much wider intervals than the trained models, and Chronos-2 forecasts a repeat of the previous day's spike that did not come. This one picture contains most of the report: decent average skill, no foresight of the onset, and real differences in recovery.

10. Uncertainty

Interval methodAll hoursSmoke at issueJune 2023Hours that became onsetsMean width, µg/m³
Raw78.6%75.1%73.2%2.0%9.8
Static conformal79.9%77.0%74.4%2.1%10.2
Adaptive conformal80.0%79.1%75.9%2.5%10.3

Coverage of nominal 80% intervals for Ensemble. Raw quantiles are somewhat over-confident. Conformal calibration fixes the average, and the adaptive version keeps coverage near 80% within the smoke stratum too. The last column is the sobering one: of the hours that became onsets, the interval contained the truth 2.5% of the time. A coverage guarantee is an average over all hours. It says nothing about the rare hours that matter most, and no calibration method can add information the model does not have.

11. Health alerts

The event is a 24-hour mean above 35.4 µg/m³ over the day following the forecast. It happens on 0.64% of monitor-days (2,387 events). "Onsets" are the 1,434 events where the previous 24 hours were below the threshold, which is when a warning is worth most.

  • If half of all alerts must be correct, Transformer + neighbours catches 54% of unhealthy days.
  • For onsets, methods that see only the monitor's own history catch at most 11% at that precision, and Transformer + neighbours catches 22%.
  • Two days ahead nothing works well: the best PR-AUC is 0.15. Warning that far out needs weather and smoke-transport information that this benchmark does not use.
  • The classifier ranks days well but its probabilities are not to be taken at face value: when it said about 14%, the event happened 28% of the time. Early stopping on the calm validation period halted it after 44 rounds, which most likely left its probabilities compressed towards the base rate. It would need recalibrating before use.

12. Limits

  • No meteorology. Wind, mixing height and smoke-plume forecasts are what operational systems use to predict onsets. Neighbour readings are a cheap stand-in and only help once the plume has reached a neighbour.
  • Monitors, not people. The panel covers 538 regulatory monitors. Dense low-cost networks would give much finer spatial context.
  • One shift. The conclusions about behaviour under shift rest on one extraordinary season, with 2024 as a single ordinary comparison year.
  • Elevated does not always mean smoke. Hours above the threshold also come from winter inversions, fireworks and dust. The benchmark does not label causes.
  • Model size. The transformer is small (1,641,392 parameters). A version with 1.1 million parameters trained earlier on the CPU reached the same validation loss, so capacity does not look like the limit, but a much larger model was not tried.
  • Foundation-model pretraining. As noted in section 7, the zero-shot models may have been pretrained on data from the test period.
  • One training run per model. Each neural model was trained once, so differences of a few hundredths of a µg/m³ between models have not been tested against run-to-run variation.

13. Concept map

ConceptWhere it appears
Data engineering at scale35.6 million raw rows reduced to a dense monitor-by-hour panel with a checksummed manifest; compact int16 storage
Missing dataNothing imputed in targets; inputs forward-filled with an explicit mask channel; completeness thresholds
Distribution shiftQuantified three ways (bulk distance, tail ratio, paired monitor-level test); used as the test condition
Hypothesis testingPaired Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction; 538 simultaneous tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control
ResamplingDay-block bootstrap intervals that respect dependence between monitors on the same day
Dimensionality reductionPrincipal components (EOFs) of the monitor-by-day anomaly matrix
Spatial statisticsGreat-circle distances, distance-binned correlogram, lagged cross-correlation, inverse-distance features
Supervised learningGlobal gradient-boosted quantile regression on a GPU; random search on a held-out period
Deep learningA patch transformer written in PyTorch: quantile loss, masking, early stopping
Foundation modelsZero-shot evaluation of pretrained forecasters on the same grid
EnsemblingEqual-weight quantile averaging across model families
Evaluation designFixed forecast grid, three scores, forecast-time strata, and the forecaster's dilemma shown on real data
Uncertainty quantificationQuantile regression, conformalized intervals, adaptive conformal inference with delayed feedback
Rare-event classificationPR-AUC, recall at fixed precision, Brier skill and a reliability check of predicted probabilities
ExplainabilityExact TreeSHAP attributions, split by regime
Software engineeringInstallable package, staged CLI, 12 leakage and protocol tests, CI workflow
